## How do we define _good_?

**Interactivity time: which do you agree with?**

 - likely to be interesting to students?
 - interesting to the lecturer(s)?
 - easy to mark?
 - easy for the students?
 - covers the latest _lit_ science / tech?
 - covers wide range of topics?
 - covers one topic in much detail?

::: {.notes}

Semi-opinionated: some learnt from EdTA course and other pedagocial teachings; some my own thoughts (which might not be sensible)

Interactivity time: everyone here has been a student (and some also teach): which do you agree with?

easiest way to mark is totally automated!
 - negatively marked MCQs?

:::

## My initial thoughts for our on-campus MSc*

####  (* different definitions of `good` for different (types of) cohorts)

 - \>1 assessment format
   - different students are good at different types of assessment, and it doesn't seem fair to penalise them for a whole module on something they might otherwise find interesting by limiting them to an assessment format which they are bad at
 - assessments should focus on understanding, not rote learning
   - this doesn't necessarily map well to predominantly exam-based assessments which we're tending back towards because of GenAI 
 - Clear progression within individual topics
   - big jumps (or inconsistency) is likely to add to confusion
 - Range of delivery formats (lectures *and* labs, and small group work in some instances)
   - we don't run any form of small group tutorials - these can be very effective when run well but takes effort
 
## Other musings

 - frequent 2 way feedback? (cf. post-it note feedback)
 - Clear rationale for inclusion of each topic in the module
 - I think it's _as_ important to also have variation across the programme
   - i.e. it's important to have both modules that do focus on one topic (e.g. MPP) and wide range of many topics (e.g. FDM)
 - should we coordinate more between modules?
   - (yes!)
 - a very alt. thought: has anyone ever attempted a whole module that is taught in the same way as a Carpentries workshop?
   - live, interactive, coding 
 - training on how to write good assessments?
   - and consistency between modules?
   - is the "difficulty value" of marks equivalent across the programme?



::: {.notes}

there's a reason Oxford / Cambridge still teach like that
